author: Osamu Dazai
introFa: کتاب «The Setting Sun» نوشته Osamu Dazai یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Setting Sun»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Japan: Land of the Rising and Setting Sun: - A Study of the Image of the Sun in Japanese Culture Elizabeth Schultz and Fumiko Yamamoto To examine the image of the sun as it appears in Japanese culture is to recognize the power of a symbol to reflect and control the aspirations of a people. In European iconography, the sun has often been humanized and familiarized; given a countenance, it may frown or smile; its rays may be long, short, sereated; its color may be white, yellow, orange, variegated. In Japan, however, the sun was deified for centuries. Its only human link was the Emperor himself, ostensibly a lineal descendant of the sun. Its principal symbolic representation was a mirror which would reflect its light directly and brilliantly. In time, the sun came to be part of commonplace Japanese iconography, a sign of material and spiritual prosperity, a sign of renewed life, but always its image was austere and absolute: round, red, with rays on occasion jutting forth symmetrically from it. Although the moon has inspired Japanese poets and artists with its lucidity, its beauty and its emphemerality, the constant sun, seldom the object of lyrical admiration, has more consistently been colored by ideological concepts than has the pale moon.’ Venerated for its brilliance, its power, its certainty, as was the imperial family, the sun remained the single image which most concretely embodied Japanese political and ethical principles until the end of the second world war. The words and ideographs for the sun in the Japanese langauge represent a variety of attitudes. The Chinese ideograph for sun is “hi,” which in Japanese denotes both “sun” and “day.” Etymology for the abstract contemporary ideograph/( 0 ) #shows its direct derivation from a literal picture of the sun. Its pronunciation today is the same as that for the word “fire,” suggesting that before they used Chinese ideographs, Japanese people regarded the sun and fire as being like aspects of nature.2 The basic ideograph, “hi,” with its close connection to natural forces, appears more frequently than other ideographs for sun in Japan’s oldest written record, the Kojiki (712 AD).j The word for Japan itself is “Ni-hon” (,: *. )a compound of a shortened form of “nichi,” which is an alternate reading of “hi” and of “hon,” “source”; the given name for Japan thus means “The Source of the Sun.” In modern compound words which have “Japanese” as their prefix, the single ideograph for sun is used; for example “Japan and America” is written L! 7 . . : “Japanese goods” 3 *c; ; “Bank of Japan . - : ; Japanese Communist Party” 3 z, . . The Japanese language, thus, continues to reflect the complete identification of the Japanese nation with the sun. Other Japanese words for the sun suggest a 117

118 Journal of Popular Culture wider range of feelings: “ten-to”( FL &- ), meaning “The Heavenly Way,” is associated with the upright character of the sun; “nichi-rin” ( i 2 2 ), meaning (‘sun-disk,’’ connotes a glorious, all-powerful celestial body; “tai- yo”( h 5;;) ) joins the ideograph for fertility with the ideograph for the positive yang principle. “Tai-yo” has come to connote a physical, almost abstract phenomenon, and it is this latter, more objective word for the sun which appears with greater frequency in contemporary usage. When one wishes to- establish a sense of familiarity with the sun, however, one addresses it with honorifics as “0-hi-sama” (“Dearly Beloved Sun”) or “0- ten-to-sama” (“Dearly Beloved Heavenly One”), but the Japanese are well aware that the sun as “tai-yo” continues its undeviating way above them. The original settlers of the Japanese archipelago set a sun goddess, Amaterasu (“Heavenly Shining One”), at the center of a mythology which they either fabricated or adapted from other southern Pacific myths.4 Of this goddess, the scholar and statesman Motoori Noringaga (1730-1801) wrote: “She is without a peer in the whole universe, casting her light to the very ends of heaven and earth and for all time. . . . This goddess is the splendor of all splendors.”5 According to Japan’s ancient records, the Kojiki and the Nihonshoki (720 AD), Amaterasu founded the Japanese nation by sending her grandson, Prince Ninigi, down from the Plains of Heaven to govern the islands. In the Kojiki, “hi”is used to designate both the names of gods in Amaterasu’s line as well as those ancient emperors who were her close descendants.6 “Hi no miko,” meaning “Prince of the Sun” is a common epithet for royal personages in the Manyoshu, the great collection of over 4000 poems compiled between the latter half of the fifth century and the middle of the eighth century. In Murasaki Shikibu’s The Tale of Genji (1022), Prince Genji is known as “the shining one” and his stepmother as “the lady of the radiant sun,”7 both sobriquets reflecting not only their personal beauty and radiance but also their imperial lineage. Thus with their divinity inherited from the sun, the Japanese imperial family became the center of a state religion, Shintoism, and absolute rulers. In them, heaven and man were thought to be one, and it was said that in comparison to the Chinese emperors, who were merely “sons of heaven,” the Japanese emperors were as heaven itself.8 Unconditional reverence consequently came to be demanded by this manifestation of the sun goddess on earth. Also recorded in the Kojiki and the Nihonshoki are the circumstances of Amaterasu’s birth and life, which have become associated with certain precepts fundamental to Shintoism and to the Japanese political and ethical system. At the heart of this system is the fear of pollution on the one hand and the reverence for purity, brightness and directness on the other hand. Prior to the birth of Amaterasu, her father, Izanagi, had to purify himself of the pollution of death and darkness. In another story, Amaterasu’s brother, Susano-o, plagued her while she was busy weaving, and in order to put an end to his obstreperous behavior, she hid herself in the darkness of a cave, thereby depriving the world of her brightness. Only when another goddess hung a mirror on a tree outside the cave did Amaterasu, catching a glimmer of her own light, come forth in all her glory. To remind him of herself, Amaterasu presented a similar mirror to Ninigi when he descended to earth to rule. Because it reflects the sun’s pure light, the mirror is said to reflect the true heart of all external phenomena and has been classified as the most important item in the imperial regalia. Of the mirror, it was written in the

Japan: Land of the Rising and Setting Sun 119 early fourteenth century, “There is never an instance when the forms of right and wrong, or good and evil, fail to show up [in it]. Its virtue consists in responding to these forms as they come. This is the basic source of correctness and ~prightness.”~ The Imperial Edicts of the seventh and eighth centuries which formed the basis for Japanese political, legal and ethical thought refer repeatedly to the value of a “bright, pure, and honest and sincere heart.”lo These values are extended into the realm of ancient aesthetics which, according to one critic, also honored above all a purity, directness and brightness whose essence was that of “high noon on a brilliant sunny day.”” Shintoism has never encouraged the construction of icons for its deities.12 The reality of the sun itself or its manifestation in the emperor were sufficient evidence of the goddess’ immanence for the ancient Japanese. Her shining mirrors, placed in many Shinto shrines, are theonly embodiment of her spirit; she does not appear in either picture or statue. Shinto shrines themselves, including the Great Shrine at Ise which is especially sacred to Amaterasu and the imperial family, are as simple and strong as nature itself, built along straight lines of unfinished wood and roofed with cedar bark. Although a traditional Japanese would have wanted to make a pilgrimage at least once in his lifetime to Ise, on a day-to- day basis he would have expressed his reverence for the sun and the emperor, not before an icon but through the simple rites of washing his face and hands and then turning toward the rising sun to clap his hands and bow. In certain parts of the country, more elaborate rituals of sun-worship, often combining with elements of Buddhism and Taoism, evolved. For example, in Tsushima, on unlucky days, village men gather together in a designated home to wait for the sun to appear; in the Tokyo area, at the time of the spring and fall equinox, people dance, chanting a prayer for the rising or the setting sun whereas in the Kyoto and Hyogo areas, people follow the sun through the course of a day, walking with it from the east to the west; on New Year’s Day, in Mie prefecture, sake is offered to the rising sun, and in Kanagawa prayers and incense are offered.13 Except for those myths concerning Amaterasu herself, folk stories concerning the sun are few. In one story, a bath-attendant informs a kitchen-maid that the moon is more important than the sun because it “appears at night when all is dark.. . . But the sun appears only in the broad daytime when no light is needed.”I4 The bath-attendant’s foolishness, of course, lies in his failure to appreciate the sun; yet the story also implies that the sun’s presence is so predictable that it may be assumed. Several stories about the sun demonstrate the presumptuousness of human attempts to manipulate it. The Kojiki and the Nihonshoki record that the first emperor of Japan, Jimmu (c. 7th century BC) on one occasion chose to fight his enemies facing the sun; consequently he was defeated, for it thus seemed he was trying to attack the sun itself. In several folk tales concerning wealthy landowners, the dangers of thwarting the sun’s course are made clear. One tale concerns a farmer’s son, who, becoming disgruntled by the numbers of peasants pestering his father for money, shoots the sun with an arrow in an attempt to keep the borrowers in the dark.15 Another tale concerns a farmer who demands that the sun shine through the night so that he can complete the rice-planting in a day. Subsequently, the fortunes of both rich men decline drastically. The landowner in the second tale nearly loses his daughter to a dragon and his rice crop at harvest-time is changed to

120 Journal of Popular Culture rushes.16 Other stories suggest the sun’s power as creator and sustainer of life, source of magic and mercy. In both the Tsushima and Kagoshima regions the story is told of a woman, impregnated by the sun, who gives birth to a son endowed with the wondrous art of devination.17 Another tale concerns three brothers who in the dark of night open the door of their home to the Man-Eating Monster, mistaking him for their mother. Although he devours the youngest boy, the two older boys escape to a peach tree where they plead, “Oh, Dearly Beloved Sun, Dearly Beloved Sun, help us please.” A chain consequently descends from the night sky, and as they climb to safety, the Monster, still pursuing, makes a similar plea only to find that the chain which drops down to him breaks, and he is dashed to death on the rocks below.18 Amaterasu’s splendor and particular promise to the Japanese people seems to become most comprehensible and accessible to them in the image of the rising sun, an image ubiquitous in Japanese culture. Because of its association with the rising sun, the East has been the direction which has been awarded special homage. Ancient tombs were often constructed so that corpses faced east,lg as were shrines so that their worshippers could confront the rising sun. In several parts of the country, high plateaus, opening to the east are called Hidaka ( ),and regarded as holy by local shrines; east of Nara, Japan’s first capital, is the area known as Hitachi, a homonym for “The Upright Sun” ( : c- ) and “The Everlasting Land” ( ,’ ,:- ).20 These are areas considered to be particularly spacious and fertile, all associated with prospects of eternity. Political prestige and power also came to be attached to the image of the rising sun and Japan’s easterly geographic position vis a vis the Asian continent. As early as 607 AD, according to Chinese legend, a Japanese envoy to China brought word that “The Emperor of the Land of the Rising Sun” sought to know how “The Emperor of the Land of the Setting Sun” fared.21 Most school-children in modern Japan are familiar with the associations between the rising sun and the great feudal warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1536-98). Not only did his mother allegedly have a dream of the rising sun at the time of his birth,LL but he is also reputed to have evoked outrage from the Chinese emperor when he addressed him in a manner similar to that of the earlier envoy. A print by the artist Toyokuni (1786- 1864) depicts a Korean princess who prays to the east, in the direction of the Land of the Rising Sun, in the hope that her white hair may become black again (Fig. 1). An examination of the image of the rising sun in popular Japanese culture reveals that, while retaining its associations with the virtues of the sun goddess and the strength of the imperial house, during the nearly 250 year period of Japan’s isolation from the rest of the world (1635-1868), the image assumed extended connotations. Thus the simple, circular emblem of the sun appeared frequently in a militaristic context. Certain warlords used it on banners to identify their troops and on equipment. Ared sun on a white or black background on fans, conical hats, and disk-shaped hats was a familiar part of the paraphernalia of military processions. The appearance of such a fan in particular originally denoted a samurai’s victory in battle (Fig. 2). Unlike the moon which waxes and wanes and which in tradi- tional Japanese iconography is frequently represented in relation to birds, flowers, snow, clouds or water, the austere sun which does not change has resisted the Japanese genius for embellishment. Thus among the ,
Japan: Land of the Rising and Setting Sun 121 Fig. 1

Japan: Land of the Rising and Setting Sun 123 several hundreds of family crests, there are, according to one source, 17 depicting the moon and 51 the stars to seven depicting the sun.23 Although it appeared on military garb, people never felt that they could be on such intimate terms with the sun that they could incorporate its image into the patterns of their ordinary clothing. The image which often appeared on the first page of a pre-modern book or print series describing a journey appropriately was that of the rising sun. The journeys designed by masters of the wood-block print, Higoshige (1797- 1858) and Eisen (1790-1848), are off to a good start as the first print in two of their journey series suggests; in both, the red hemisphere of the sun on the horizon echoes the arcs in the background of the Nihonbashi ( 0 &&),the point from which most Tokyo-based journeys began (Fig. 3). The begin- ning of the year and the hopes associated with it, however, prompted the greatest variety in the representations of the rising sun. Although the round red image itself never varies, for the New Year’s celebrations it is shown in conjunction with several other conventional Japanese motifs which have auspicious implications, signifying longevity and material and spiritual prosperity. In conjunction with the crane, tortoise and elderly couple, it conveys hope for a long and happy life with the pine and ocean, it conveys hope for the perpetual renewal of life; and with the treasure ship, it conveys hope for material prosperity. Not only does it appear on scrolls and prints at the New Year (Fig. 4), but it also appears on cake-box covers, toys and greeting cards (Figs. 5 & 6); perhaps little boys are especially blessed in being able to raise their own rising suns at New Years by flying kites with the emblem printed boldly on them (Fig. 7). When, rarely, the rising sun has been pictured at the conclusion of a work, its generally auspicious connotations are intensified by specifically moral implications. The rising sun on the last page of a workis a guarantee that justice and the good have triumphed, that heaven has sanctioned action on earth. Thus in the last print in a series describing the events in the famous story of the Forty-Seven Ronin, Hiroshige I1 (1826-69) has drawn the triumphant warriors with the severed head of the man responsible for their lord’s death in front of them and the sun rising behind them. On the final page of a well-known children’s story, the sun rises over the sea behind the cunning rabbit in his wooden boat to sanction his triumphantly overturning the cruel badger in his mud boat. In time, the values associated with the rising sun came to embrace a work ethic familiar to Protestant cultures. The ritual of morning sun- worship necessitating early rising became the basis for a code promoting physical well-being, hard work and material gain. More than a dozen Japanese proverbs, such as “Fortune comes to the family that rises early,” “The early riser earns three cents,” “A sleepyhead is a born loser,” guarantee profit for the early riser. Six A.M. calisthentics have been a common part of the day’s activities for the Japanese for many years, with instructions nowadays being given over the loudspeaker in rural town squares, in school playgrounds everywhere and, of course, by radio and TV. A World War I1 radio exercise song expresses the sense of how invigorating the morning sun might be: Bathed in the light of the brilliant morning sun Flex and stretch your arms and limbs.

Japan: Land of the Rising and Setting Sun 129 The radio is calling, “One, two, three!’’24 Yamamoto Kanae’s 1906 print shows a young woodcutter brimming with vitality as he stands flexing his muscles beneath the radiant sun. Children with round red cheeks are said to reflect the healthy influence of the round red sun. Popular songs such as the following continue to emphasize that the rising sun is the source not only of Japan’s physical well-being but also for the country’s spiritual well-being: ’Tis morning, morning The morning sun is rising Today again, the joyous sun is rising. Get up, everyone, get up in happiness. Our hearts are bright and clear in the morning. ’Tis morning, morning The morning sun is rising. The sun is rising all over Japan.L5 ... Recent study of the myths surrounding the sun goddess has revealed them to be stories used by the nobility to authenticate the divinity of the emperor and to insure undivided support among his people.26 That the image of the rising sun has continued to engender the concept of a unified Japan is implicit in such popular songs as that quoted above. The power of the image as a unifying device was dramatized in the mid-nineteenth century when it was chosen as the emblem for the flag of a nation newly restored to internal harmony by the Emperor Meiji and by the conclusion of the policy of isolation. The flag would distinguish Japanese ships from foreign vessels encouraged to enter its harbors for the first time and would proclaim the sovereignity of the Japanese people on foreign missions. Following its adoption as the country’s official flag in 1870, the “hi-no- maru,” meaning “circle of sun” was flown from gateways on every political or military occasion, with a separate flag, a sun streaming rays, being developed especially for the navy. With the outbreak of World War 11, the image of the rising sun became the most visible symbol for galvanizing the Japanese nation. Centuries before, Motoori Norinaga had foreseen that because of the sun goddess’ “special dispensation” to Japan, that land was destined to rule over other lands; he asserted that because Japan is “the native land of the Heaven- Shining Goddess who casts her light over all countries in the four seas . . . [it] is the source and fountainhead of all countries, and in all matters it excels all the other^."^' Norinaga’s assertions paved the way for the militarists of the second world war to appropriate the sun to their imperialistic ends. With the particular blessings of the sun, it seemed Japan could rightfully conquer the earth as such wartime songs as the following indicate: This morning The clouds are mounting Under the rising sun. Great Japan arose In determination and in justice. So take up your scourging gun and sword.2x

130 Journal of Popular Culture Soldiers departed for battle wearing flags given to them by loved ones tied diagnally across their chests; they entered battle wearing head-bands emblazoned with the rising sun and brave words of old; their planes were marked with the rising sun, and one of their ill-fated kamikaze suicide units was called “The Morning Sun.” Children made packets to send to the soldiers which included small “hi-no-maru” flags and were made to take lunches to school which resembled the “hi-no-maru”: white rice with a pickled red plum in the center. The emblem of the rising sun was evidence of the soldier’s friends’ hope that he would triumph in battle and of his country’s assurance that his endeavor was conducted in the name of justice and righteousness. When the soldier was killed, the government sent his family a small flag, signifying that he had not died in vain, for his sacrifice strengthened the nation. With the end of the war, however, Japan’s rising sun quite literally set. Not only did images of the setting sun come into prominence, but as anti- imperial and anti-military sentiment evolved, the sun itself came to be represented as a hostile force. The sun’s austerity which had been inspiration for righteousness now came to be interpreted as brutal indifference. Allusions to and representations of the setting sun had long co-existed in the Japanese mind with those of the rising sun although the latter had always been in the ascendant. Unlike the rising sun which had nurtured a spirit of triumph and hope, prosperity and energy, righteousness and unity, popular depictions of the setting sun emphasized the sorrows of failure and despair, loneliness and death. Thus, in the repertoire of the Noh theater, among those plays dealing with warriors, the three plays concerning the triumphant warrior use a fan with the image of the rising sun whereas the six plays concerning the defeated warrior use a fan with the image of the setting sun.29 A World War I1 song evokes a rare feeling of loss through its reference to the setting sun: Hundreds of miles away from our land, Far, far away in Manchuria, Illuminated by the crimson evening sun, My friend is here beneath a stone On the edge of a field.:’” It might be possible to speculate that images of the rising sun, so much more predominant in Japanese popular culture than those of the setting sun, have been associated with the indigenous tradition of Shintoism whereas the images of the moon and of the setting sun have been associated with Buddhism, which was brought to Japan in the sixth century and which stresses the emphemeral nature of life and the inconsequentiality of the political and material world. However, if any such connection could be argued, it must be noted that as the traditional image of the rising sun came to be challenged, the image of the setting sun came to be corrupted, appearing as a backdrop for the sentimental figure of the foresaken lover. A certain amount of oblique criticism of the patriotic and materialistic values inspired by the rising sun existed before the second world war. For example, Yokomitsu Riichi’s 1923 mythic fantasy, Sun Disk, describes the process by which the Princess Himiko comes to desire her transformation into the sun in order to take a bloody vengeance on those who had brutalized

Japan: Land of the Rising and Setting Sun 131 her, and Tokunaga Sunao’s 1929 novel, The Sunless Town, suggests that the warmth and largesse of the sun which should be shared by all is controlled by the wealthy. Even Tanizaki Junichiro’s well-known “In Praise of Shadows” (1933-34), which eulogizes the muted beauty of shadows in traditional Japanese culture, might be considered a subtle criticism of the absolute values implied by the sun. Following the war, however, an overtly vigorous criticism of these values became apparent in the evocations of the image of the setting sun and of the sun itself. Thus in the conclusion of three post-war novels-Dazai Osamu’s The Setting Sun (1947), Umezaki Haruo’s The End of the Day (1947) and Ooka Shohei’s Fires on the Plain (1952)-the sun sets, and implicitly the old morality comes crashing down with it. In these works, the principal characters, who have either betrayed others or been betrayed by them, have a final vision similar to that of Ooka’s narrator, who in a nearly sunless world struggles to create a new sense of values: In the dark sky the sun glows still darker, like obsidian.. . . Suddenly I understand. I know now why [the dead people] are laughing. I have killed them, to be sure, but I have not eaten them. I killed them because of war, God, chance-forces outside myself; but it was assuredly because of my own will that I did not eat them. This is why in their company I can now gaze a t that dark sun in this country of the dead. Thus the traditional sense of failure, despair, loneliness and death associated with the setting sun is intensified by a sense of devastating chaos which obliterates the absolute values of the rising sun. Miyoshi Toyoichiro’s poem “The Prisoner” is typical of poems being written by young Japanese who evoke the imagery of sunset to imply that the glorious pursuit of the sun results in an Icarus-like fall: the sunset of today so beautiful it saddens, the shape of one small bird in agony, The shade of the distress of escape -vomiting blood and trembling trembling and coughing- that falls between the sky and ground[.]J2 The setting sun itself becomes the subject of scorn in Taniuchi Rokuro’s post-war poster which dramatizes the rampant commercialism of modern Japan when half a Lucky-Strike package is substituted on the horizon for the setting sun.33 When the sun is represented at the height of day in post-war literature, it scorches, parches and destroys. Hara Tamiki in his short story “Summer Flowers” (1947) remembers that the sun was blazing in Hiroshima the day the atomic bomb was dropped, and the resulting flames and blood seemed an extension of that unnatural phenomenon. Iijima Koichi’s poem “The End of the War to End All Wars” also relates the red of the sun to the blood of the war-dead: The sky holds its head as though it had eaten stone, plunged now in grief The bloodshed’s stopped But all the blood’s still circling in the sky.,jd

132 Journal of Popular Culture Although he ultimately renews his understanding of the traditional values associated with the sun in Sun and Steel (1965), when Mishima Yukio looks back upon the war period in his work, he also identifies the sun with meaningless death: That same sun, as the days turned to months and the months to years, had become associated with a pervasive corruption and destruction. In part it was the way it gleamed so encouragingly on the wings of planes leaving on missions, on forests of bayonets, on the badges of military capes, on theembroidery of military banners; but still more, far more, it was the way it glistened on the blood flowing ceaselessly from the flesh.. . . Holding sway over corruption, leading youth in droves to its death in tropical seas and countrysides, the sun lorded it over that vast rusty-red ruin that stretched away to the distant horizon.,’Is Abe Kobo’s view of the sun in his short story “Magic Chalk” (1950) is ambiguous. He associates the sun on the one hand with knowledge, inevitability and common humanity and on the other hand with the destruction of pleasure, beauty and the artist’s individual struggle to create. If the story’s conclusion suggests that the sun-or the new political ideology-must prevail, it also implies that the sacrifice of the precious, private and gentle creations of the artist to the sun’s overwhelming power of creativity is grievous. Thus in the years following the war the sun was represented as inspiring chaos rather than unity, death rather than life, materialism rather than healthy prosperity, and injustice and violence rather than righteousness. Post-war cartoons by Akase Genpei, for example, show the sun shining or the “hi-no-maru” flag flying over a variety of violent atrocities-wanton plundering, killing, raping-as if to sanction them. 16 Ishihara Shintaro’s best-selling novel, The Season of the Sun, and the movie based on it spawned a term for the post-war generation which was its subject: “the sun tribe.” Instead of being characterized by the ancient virtues of the sun goddess, however, these young people were committed to violence, nihilism and narcissism. Seeking to reverse his culture’s mockery of the sun and to reinstate it as the embodiment of positive traditional values, Mishima explored its symbolic implications in his writing and in his personal actions. In Sun and Steel, he describes the process by which he overcame his youthful despair with the sun as a death-ridden symbol; he gradually developed an appreciation for a life strengthened by discipline in the ancient martial arts and by physical exercise in the open air, under the sun’s light. Fulfillment of this ideal life is realized by the young hero of Runaway Horses (1969), the second novel in the tetralogy Mishima finished writing just prior to his suicide. Attempting to lead a revolution against decadent government officials, the youth fails and commits ritual suicide; but as he dies, he sees before his eyes that most potent of traditional Japanese symbols for righteousness, hope and triumph: “The sun will not rise for some time,” Isao said to himself, “and I can’t afford to wait. There is no shining disk climbing upward. There is no noble pine to shelter me. Nor is there a sparkling sea.” . . . Then, with a powerful thrust of his arm, he plunged the knife into his stomach. The instant that the blade tore open his flesh, the bright disk of the sun soared up and exploded behind his eyelids.

Japan: Land of the Rising and Setting Sun 133 In 1970 Mishima appeared before the Japanese Self-Defense Force to address them out of his urgent sense that the military should take the lead in restoring the nation to the old morality. He wore a head-band marked with the rising sun in the manner of Japanese soldiers of the past, and following his speech, he performed the supreme sacrifice of committing ritual suicide. Perhaps Mishima’s final act can best be understood as his personal interpretation of Japan’s traditional political and ethical code, of Japan’s special relationship with the sun. Without taking such extreme measures, contemporary Japanese also continue to acknowledge their culture’s special relationship with the sun. Not only does the ideograph for the sun remain an intrinsic part of Japan’s name, not only is the image of the sun ubiquitous at times of celebration and through the presence of the national flag, but for the contemporary Japanese, as for their ancestors, the sun continues to be round and red, absolute and austere. They may show their respect for this sun and for its particular blessing on them as a people by journeying to Mt. Shichimen from which they can contemplate it rising in full splendor over Mt. Fuji. Or they may recall the mesmerizing power of symbols as they contemplate the frequently reproduced 1965 photograph, originally published in the Asahi (“Morning Sun”) newspaper’s nationally circulated picture magazine, of the sun setting behind the blasted, skeletal dome of Hiroshima’s Industrial Promotion Hall.38 Notes (Throughout the essay when Japanese names are cited, the familyname appears before thegiven name.) ‘For example, allusions to the moon in Japan’s first great literary work, the Manyoshu, and in waka, choka and haiku poetry far outnumber those to the sun, and there is no series of wood- block prints based on the sun’s image comparable to Yoshitoshi’s (1839-1892) One-Hundred Aspects of the Moon. ‘Tanaka Katsuhiko “Hi ni Kansuru Mono no Goyen” in Nrhon Kodai-bunka nu Tankyu, ed.
